body:
Traditional classification of musical instruments

Indian musical instruments are traditionally divided into 4 principal categories according to the physical means by which they produce sound. This classification is associated with the ancient musical and dramatic tradition represented by Bharata Muni's Natya Shastra.

1. Tata Vadya: String instruments

In string instruments, sound is produced by the vibration of stretched strings. The strings may be plucked, bowed or struck.

  • Plucked strings: Sitar, sarod, veena and tanpura.
  • Bowed strings: Sarangi and violin.
  • Struck strings: Santoor, whose strings are struck with small wooden mallets.

The sitar has a long fretted neck, while the sarod has a fretless playing surface. The sarangi is a bowed string instrument traditionally associated with Hindustani vocal accompaniment. The Saraswati veena is particularly associated with Carnatic music.

2. Sushira Vadya: Wind instruments

Wind instruments produce sound through the vibration of air. Important examples include the bansuri, shehnai and nadaswaram.

  • Bansuri: A flute, traditionally made of bamboo.
  • Shehnai: A double-reed wind instrument particularly associated with northern India.
  • Nadaswaram: A double-reed wind instrument particularly associated with South Indian temples, ceremonies and classical music.

3. Avanaddha Vadya: Membrane instruments

These instruments produce sound primarily through the vibration of a stretched membrane.

  • Tabla: A pair of separate drums, comprising the dayan and bayan.
  • Pakhawaj: A double-headed barrel-shaped drum traditionally associated with Dhrupad.
  • Mridangam: A double-headed drum that serves as a principal percussion instrument in Carnatic music.
  • Tavil: A drum frequently associated with nadaswaram performances.
  • Kanjira: A small frame drum used in Carnatic music.

4. Ghana Vadya: Solid instruments

These instruments produce sound primarily through the vibration of their own solid material rather than a stretched string or membrane.

Examples include the manjira, a pair of small cymbals; the ghatam, an earthen pot used as a percussion instrument; and the morsing, a metal jaw harp.

Not all percussion instruments belong to Avanaddha Vadya. The tabla and mridangam use stretched membranes, whereas the ghatam produces sound through the vibration of its solid body.

Recognising important instruments

Instruments may be distinguished by their construction as well as their musical function. A tabla consists of 2 separate drums, while a pakhawaj or mridangam is a single double-headed drum. A ghatam is a pot without a stretched membrane. A santoor uses struck strings and is therefore a string instrument despite its striking method of playing.

Important musician-instrument associations

MusicianInstrument
Pandit Ravi ShankarSitar
Ustad Amjad Ali KhanSarod
Ustad Bismillah KhanShehnai
Pandit Shivkumar SharmaSantoor
Pandit Hariprasad ChaurasiaBansuri
Ustad Alla RakhaTabla

These musicians are particularly associated with the Hindustani classical tradition. Instruments such as the flute and violin, however, are also important in Carnatic music.

Prelims focus

  • Tata means string instruments; Sushira means wind instruments.
  • Avanaddha instruments use membranes; Ghana instruments use vibrating solid material.
  • Pakhawaj is traditionally associated with Dhrupad.
  • Mridangam and ghatam are important Carnatic percussion instruments.
  • Bismillah Khan: shehnai; Shivkumar Sharma: santoor; Amjad Ali Khan: sarod.
  • Trap: Santoor is a string instrument, not a membrane instrument.

[References: IGNCA, Sansad ki Kala: Sangeet Deergha, musical instrument classification panel; Metropolitan Museum of Art, Allen Roda, Musical Instruments of the Indian Subcontinent, 2009; NIOS, Indian Culture and Heritage, Secondary Course 223, Chapter 12; Kerala State Council of Educational Research and Training, Class 12 Music, Masters in Music: Hindustani Instrumentalists, p. 121. Consulted 25 November 2026.]

title: Indian Musical Instruments: Classification, Identification and Famous Exponents

body:
Major texts in the history of Indian music

Indian musical knowledge developed through oral traditions as well as written treatises. Several Sanskrit works provide important evidence of the development of musical concepts before and during the emergence of Hindustani and Carnatic music.

TextAuthor or traditionSignificance
Sama VedaVedic traditionMelodic religious chanting
Natya ShastraBharata MuniAncient dramatic and musical theory
BrihaddeshiMatanga MuniImportant early explanation of raga
Sangita MakarandaNaradaMusical notes, ragas and instruments
Sangita RatnakaraSharngadevaCommon theoretical heritage of Indian classical music
Sangita ParijataAhobala17th-century musical theory
Chaturdandi PrakashikaVenkatamakhinTheoretical foundation of the 72-mela system

Sangita Ratnakara

The Sangita Ratnakara, composed by Sharngadeva in the 13th century, occupies a particularly important position in Indian musical history.

Sharngadeva was associated with Devagiri, later known as Daulatabad, in present-day Maharashtra. His work deals with musical theory and practice, including notes, ragas, rhythm, musical instruments and dance.

It was written before the modern Hindustani and Carnatic systems acquired their later distinct forms. Consequently, both traditions recognise its importance in their common theoretical heritage.

Sangita Parijata

Ahobala composed the Sangita Parijata in the 17th century, conventionally dated to 1665 in Gujarat's school textbook. It is an important treatise concerned with musical notes and ragas in the northern Indian musical tradition.

Amir Khusro: Delhi Sultanate period

Amir Khusro (1253–1325), also spelled Amir Khusrau, was a poet, scholar and musician associated with the Delhi Sultanate. He lived during the reigns of several Delhi Sultans, including Alauddin Khalji.

His literary and cultural achievements earned him the title Tuti-e-Hind, meaning Parrot of India.

Amir Khusro was a disciple of the Chishti Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya. His musical heritage is closely associated with the interaction of Indian and Persian cultural traditions and with Sufi devotional music.

Tradition associates him particularly with Qawwali and Tarana. Claims that he invented the sitar or tabla are widely repeated but are not securely established by historical evidence.

Amir Khusro belongs to the Delhi Sultanate period, not the Mughal period. Traditional attributions concerning musical inventions should be distinguished from historically established facts.

Tansen: Mughal period

Miyan Tansen was a major Hindustani classical musician of the 16th century and a celebrated musician at the court of the Mughal emperor Akbar.

He is traditionally counted among Akbar's 9 distinguished court figures, collectively known as the Navaratnas. His musical career is closely associated with the Dhrupad tradition, and traditional accounts identify Swami Haridas as an important musical teacher.

Ragas traditionally associated with Tansen include Miyan ki Malhar and Miyan ki Todi.

Stories describing Tansen lighting lamps by singing Raga Deepak or bringing rain through a raga belong to musical folklore. They express his extraordinary reputation but should not be interpreted as scientifically established effects of music.

Chronological relationship with Tyagaraja

Tyagaraja, the celebrated Carnatic composer, lived from 1767 to 1847, considerably later than both Amir Khusro and Tansen.

The sequence is important because it connects 3 different historical contexts: the Delhi Sultanate, Mughal musical patronage and the later development of the Carnatic compositional tradition.

Prelims focus

  • Natya Shastra: Bharata Muni; Brihaddeshi: Matanga Muni.
  • Sangita Ratnakara: Sharngadeva, 13th century, Devagiri.
  • Sangita Parijata: Ahobala, 17th century.
  • Amir Khusro: Delhi Sultanate, Nizamuddin Auliya, Tuti-e-Hind.
  • Chronological order: Amir Khusro, Tansen, Tyagaraja.
  • Trap: Tansen was associated with Akbar, not Alauddin Khalji.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, 2020 English reprint, Chapter 2, Music, p. 12; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Chapter 6, pp. 155–157; NIOS, Indian Culture and Heritage, Secondary Course 223, Chapter 12, pp. 170–173; NIOS, Hindustani Music, Chapter 8, Brief Study of Contents of Sangeet Parijat; IGNCA, Sansad ki Kala: Sangeet Deergha, Miyan Tansen and Swami Haridas panels; Dileep Karanth, Amir Khusrau's Contributions to Indian Music: A Preliminary Survey, Sangeet Natak, 2008. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

title: Historical Development: Important Texts, Amir Khusro and Tansen

body:
Development of the Carnatic tradition

Carnatic classical music developed predominantly in southern India through the interaction of devotional movements, musical scholarship, temple traditions and royal patronage.

Its development was influenced by the long tradition of devotional singing in southern India. Composers expressed religious and philosophical ideas through musical works in regional languages and Sanskrit.

Purandara Dasa

Purandara Dasa, who lived during the 15th and 16th centuries, is widely honoured as the Father of Carnatic Music or the Pitamaha of Carnatic Music.

He belonged to the Haridasa devotional tradition of Karnataka and composed numerous devotional songs, particularly in Kannada.

His contribution was not limited to composition. He is credited with systematising graded musical exercises that established an influential foundation for teaching Carnatic music.

Purandara Dasa was an important predecessor of the Carnatic Trinity. He is not one of its 3 members.

The Carnatic Trinity

The Carnatic Trinity consists of 3 major composers whose works profoundly influenced the modern Carnatic musical repertoire. They flourished during the late 18th and early 19th centuries and are associated by birth with Tiruvarur in present-day Tamil Nadu.

Tyagaraja

Tyagaraja (1767–1847), also spelled Thyagaraja, composed devotional works predominantly in Telugu. His compositions frequently express devotion to Rama.

His best-known groups of compositions include the Pancharatna Kritis, meaning 5 gem-like compositions.

Although born in Tiruvarur, Tyagaraja is especially associated with Tiruvaiyaru in Tamil Nadu, where his musical and devotional legacy is commemorated.

Muthuswami Dikshitar

Muthuswami Dikshitar composed extensively in Sanskrit. His works frequently concern Hindu deities, sacred places and philosophical themes.

His compositions include the celebrated Kamalamba Kritis. His repertoire reflects close connections between Carnatic music, Sanskrit learning and devotional traditions.

Syama Sastri

Syama Sastri, also spelled Shyama Shastri, composed devotional works particularly associated with the goddess Kamakshi.

He composed in languages including Telugu and Sanskrit and is especially remembered for his contribution to the Swarajati form.

ComposerLanguage associationImportant association
TyagarajaPredominantly TeluguRama; Pancharatna Kritis
Muthuswami DikshitarPredominantly SanskritKamalamba Kritis
Syama SastriTelugu and SanskritKamakshi; Swarajati

Principal forms of Carnatic music

Kriti

The Kriti is a central compositional form of Carnatic music. It combines a raga, a rhythmic framework and composed lyrics. Many kritis have devotional or philosophical themes.

A typical kriti has 3 principal sections:

  • Pallavi: The opening section containing the principal musical and lyrical idea.
  • Anupallavi: A subsequent section that develops the opening idea.
  • Charanam: A concluding or extended section of the composition.

Individual compositions may vary from this typical structure.

Varnam

Varnam is an important Carnatic compositional form used in musical training and concert presentation. It illustrates characteristic features of a raga and is frequently performed near the beginning of a concert.

Kirtana

Kirtana is a song form particularly associated with devotional expression and praise. It emphasises the communication of a devotional theme through music.

Tillana

Tillana is a lively composition characterised by rhythmic syllables. It is frequently presented towards the end of Carnatic concerts and is also used in classical dance.

It has a broad functional resemblance to the Hindustani Tarana, although the 2 forms belong to different musical traditions.

Swarajati

Swarajati is a form combining musical notes and lyrical passages. It has roles in musical training and concert performance. Syama Sastri's Swarajatis are important examples of this compositional tradition.

Prelims focus

  • Purandara Dasa: Father of Carnatic Music; Kannada devotional compositions.
  • Carnatic Trinity: Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri.
  • All 3 members of the Trinity were born in Tiruvarur.
  • Tyagaraja: 1767–1847, Telugu, Rama and Pancharatna Kritis.
  • The typical Kriti consists of Pallavi, Anupallavi and Charanam.
  • Trap: Purandara Dasa is not a member of the Carnatic Trinity.

[References: IGNCA, Sansad ki Kala: Sangeet Deergha, Purandara Dasa and Carnatic Trinity panels; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, Classical Carnatic Music; Akashvani News, Aaj Savere, discussion of Tyagaraja and the Carnatic Trinity; Music Academy Madras, 51st Conference Souvenir, 1977, V. Raghavan, Sri Syama Sastri; Journal of the Music Academy, Volume 40, 1970, The Dikshaitars, pp. 194–207; Darbar, Performance Format for Carnatic Concerts: Sections of a Kutcheri. Consulted 25 November 2026.]
